meta.name: Theological Archive - Saul's Podship
meta.description: 100 Tough Theology Questions + 1,000 Book-by-Book Bible Study Questions

tough_questions.question: Where did God come from?
tough_questions.short_answer: God did not come from anywhere. He is uncreated and eternal — the one being who simply is, from whom everything else derives its existence.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.

Catholic.summary: Aseity: God is ipsum esse subsistens, subsistent being itself, with no cause outside himself (Aquinas, ST I.3.4).
Catholic.detail: Aquinas argues that in every creature essence and existence are distinct — a thing can be conceived without existing — whereas in God alone essence is existence. This is why the Fourth Lateran and First Vatican Councils speak of God as absolutely simple and immutable.

Orthodox.summary: God's essence is utterly unknowable; we know him only through his uncreated energies, never as a caused being.
Orthodox.detail: The Cappadocian Fathers drew the decisive line between God's ousia (essence), which is entirely beyond creaturely knowledge, and his energeiai (energies), by which he genuinely acts upon and is known by creation.

Protestant.summary: Scripture never argues for God's origin because he has none — 'from everlasting to everlasting' is a denial of the question's premise.
Protestant.detail: The Reformers treated divine aseity less as a metaphysical thesis than as a pastoral one. If God depends on nothing, then his promises depend on nothing either.

Anglican.summary: Article I: God is 'everlasting, without body, parts, or passions' — infinite in power, wisdom and goodness.
Anglican.detail: Hooker develops the point in the Laws, arguing that God's law to himself is his own being, so obedience to God is never submission to arbitrary power.

Pentecostal.summary: The eternal God is also the present God: the same 'I AM' who never began is the one who meets the believer now.
Pentecostal.detail: The 'I AM' of Exodus 3:14 functions in Pentecostal spirituality as a present-tense name, which is why testimony language so often moves from what God did in Scripture straight to what he is doing now.

tough_questions.question: If God is good, why is there evil and suffering?
tough_questions.short_answer: Scripture does not explain evil away; it says God is neither its author nor its victim, and that in Christ he entered suffering rather than merely permitting it.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And we know that to them that love God all things work together for good, even to them that are called according to his purpose.

Catholic.summary: Evil is privatio boni — a lack of due good, not a substance; God permits it only to draw greater good from it.
Catholic.detail: Catholic teaching distinguishes physical evil, permitted within a world of genuine secondary causes, from moral evil, which arises solely from the misuse of created freedom.
Catholic.quote: Evil is the privation of a good.

Orthodox.summary: Evil is the misuse of created freedom; the cross and resurrection heal creation rather than merely justify God.
Orthodox.detail: The Paschal troparion — 'trampling down death by death' — states the answer liturgically: God's response to evil is not an explanation but an invasion.

Protestant.summary: Free will, the fall, and God's sovereign purpose are held together: Gen 50:20 and Rom 8:28 refuse both fatalism and chance.
Protestant.detail: Reformed thought distinguishes God's decretive will from his preceptive will, allowing Scripture to say both that Joseph's brothers sinned and that God meant it for good.

Anglican.summary: A pastoral rather than speculative answer: the Church laments with Job and trusts without a full theodicy.
Anglican.detail: The Prayer Book gives the sufferer the Psalter — including Psalm 88 — rather than an argument, on the conviction that the Church's first duty to the afflicted is to give them words, not reasons.

Pentecostal.summary: Suffering is real but not final; the Spirit both comforts in it and breaks into it with healing and deliverance.
Pentecostal.detail: Pentecostal theology tends to read suffering as contested territory rather than settled providence: much of it is attributed to a real enemy whose works Christ came to destroy.

tough_questions.question: How can God be three Persons and one God?
tough_questions.short_answer: One divine essence subsisting in three distinct Persons — not three gods, not one Person in three masks. The distinction is of relation, not of substance.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Go ye therefore, and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Catholic.summary: Persons are subsistent relations; the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (filioque).
Catholic.detail: Augustine's De Trinitate supplies the Western grammar: the Persons are distinguished only by their relations of origin — the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Spirit spirated.

Orthodox.summary: The Father is the sole fountainhead (monarchia); the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son.
Orthodox.detail: The East begins not with the one essence but with the Father as sole source, from whom the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds.

Protestant.summary: Fully affirmed as the Nicene faith, defended from Scripture rather than from conciliar authority alone.
Protestant.detail: The Reformers received Nicaea wholesale and defended it exegetically rather than by conciliar appeal — Calvin's Institutes I.13 assembles the biblical case at length.

Anglican.summary: Article I confesses three Persons of one substance, power and eternity; the Athanasian Creed is retained.
Anglican.detail: Its uncompromising clauses — 'neither confounding the Persons, nor dividing the Substance' — were kept precisely because the errors they exclude recur in every generation.

Pentecostal.summary: Trinitarian Pentecostals hold the classic creed; Oneness Pentecostals dissent, teaching modes of one Person.
Pentecostal.detail: The Oneness–Trinitarian split of 1913-16 was the most serious doctrinal division in Pentecostal history, turning on baptismal formula and the nature of the Godhead.

tough_questions.question: Did God create sin?
tough_questions.short_answer: God created beings capable of choosing, and that capacity was good. Sin arose from the misuse of that freedom, not from a defect in what God made.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempteth no man.

Catholic.summary: God permits but never causes moral evil; he is not the deficient cause of the defective act.
Catholic.detail: Aquinas explains that God is the cause of the act of sin insofar as it is an act (all being comes from God), but not of its defect, which arises from the deficient created will.

Orthodox.summary: Sin is a movement away from being toward non-being — a parasite on the good, with no created substance.
Orthodox.detail: Following Athanasius and Maximus, Orthodoxy treats sin as a movement toward non-being — a failure of the creature to move toward the God for whom it was made.

Protestant.summary: Reformed theology distinguishes God's decree to permit from his authorship: he ordains that sin be, without sinning.
Protestant.detail: The Westminster Confession III.1 states the position with unusual care: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, 'yet so as thereby neither is God the author of sin.'

Anglican.summary: Article IX locates the fault in the corrupted nature of man, not in the Creator.
Anglican.detail: The Article's language of concupiscence remaining even in the regenerate keeps Anglican spirituality realistic about ongoing struggle.

Pentecostal.summary: Emphasis falls on the reality of Satan as tempter and on the Spirit's power to break sin's dominion.
Pentecostal.detail: The personal agency of the tempter — 'your adversary the devil' is treated as a genuine actor rather than a symbol.

tough_questions.question: Why did God allow Satan to exist?
tough_questions.short_answer: Satan is a creature, not a rival deity. His existence is permitted within strict limits, and his defeat is already accomplished at the cross.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And the LORD said unto Satan, Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand.

Catholic.summary: The devil's fall was a definitive angelic choice; his power is real but permitted and bounded.
Catholic.detail: The Church nonetheless insists the devil's power is finite and permitted: 'he cannot prevent the building up of God's reign' (CCC 395).

Orthodox.summary: The demonic is engaged chiefly through asinesis, prayer and the Church's exorcistic rites.
Orthodox.detail: The Philokalia catalogues the logismoi — intrusive thoughts by which the enemy works — and prescribes watchfulness (nepsis) and the Jesus Prayer as the ordinary defence.

Protestant.summary: Satan is a defeated foe whose remaining activity serves, unwillingly, the purposes of God.
Protestant.detail: Luther's counsel was characteristically blunt: the devil is defeated, and 'one little word shall fell him.'

Anglican.summary: Renunciation of 'the devil and all his works' remains central to the baptismal liturgy.
Anglican.detail: Anglican deliverance ministry is regulated: since 1975 English dioceses have required that any exorcism be authorised by the bishop.

Pentecostal.summary: Spiritual warfare is a practised discipline: binding, resisting and casting out in Jesus' name.
Pentecostal.detail: Critiques inside Pentecostalism warn that an overdeveloped demonology can eclipse both human responsibility and the finished work of the cross.

tough_questions.question: Is God's sovereignty compatible with human free will?
tough_questions.short_answer: Scripture asserts both without resolving the mechanism: God works genuinely, and human choices are genuinely ours and genuinely accountable.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God which worketh in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.

Catholic.summary: Grace perfects nature; free cooperation with grace is required and itself enabled by grace.
Catholic.detail: The Molinist–Thomist controversy (the Congregatio de Auxiliis, 1597-1607) debated this question so fiercely that Rome finally forbade either side to call the other heretical.

Orthodox.summary: Synergy — God and the human person work together, without grace overriding personhood.
Orthodox.detail: The East insists this does not divide credit — grace remains wholly prior and wholly gift — but preserves the person as a genuine agent.

Protestant.summary: Calvinists stress effectual grace and monergism; Arminians stress resistible grace and libertarian freedom.
Protestant.detail: The Synod of Dort (1618-19) answered the Arminian Remonstrance with the five heads later summarised as TULIP.

Anglican.summary: Article X: we have no power to do good works without the grace of God preventing us.
Anglican.detail: The formulary is deliberately broad enough to house both Calvinist and Arminian Anglicans, as it has since the seventeenth century.

Pentecostal.summary: Strongly emphasises free response to the gospel and to the Spirit's continual invitation.
Pentecostal.detail: The 'whosoever will' of Revelation 22:17 functions almost as a Pentecostal motto, and the altar call presupposes a genuine and immediate power of response.

tough_questions.question: What does it mean that Jesus is fully God and fully man?
tough_questions.short_answer: One Person in two complete natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division or separation — the Chalcedonian definition of AD 451.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.

Catholic.summary: Chalcedon is dogma; the communicatio idiomatum permits saying God suffered in the flesh.
Catholic.detail: Because there is one Person, what is true of either nature may be predicated of the Person.

Orthodox.summary: Chalcedon affirmed, with strong stress on two wills and two energies (Sixth Council).
Orthodox.detail: Maximus the Confessor was mutilated and exiled for this position before it was vindicated.

Protestant.summary: Held firmly; the kenosis of Phil 2 is read as veiling, not surrender, of divine attributes.
Protestant.detail: Lutherans and Reformed christology diverged over the genus maiestaticum.

Anglican.summary: Article II: two whole and perfect natures joined together in one Person, never to be divided.
Anglican.detail: Article II's phrase is verbally close to Chalcedon and was framed to exclude both Anabaptist and continental speculations.

Pentecostal.summary: Practical emphasis: the Spirit-anointed humanity of Jesus is the model for Spirit-filled ministry.
Pentecostal.detail: This 'Spirit christology' grounds the movement's expectation that the same Spirit enables the same works in the church.

tough_questions.question: Did Jesus have to die, or was there another way?
tough_questions.short_answer: The New Testament treats the cross as necessary given God's justice and mercy together — Gethsemane's 'if it be possible' received no alternative.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And according to the law, I may almost say, all things are cleansed with blood, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.

Catholic.summary: Satisfaction: Christ offers to the Father a reparation of infinite worth for the offence of sin.
Catholic.detail: Anselm's Cur Deus Homo supplies the Western framework: sin is an infinite offence against infinite honour, which only one who is both God and man can repair.

Orthodox.summary: Christus Victor and recapitulation: death is destroyed from within by the death of the Deathless One.
Orthodox.detail: The East never adopted Anselm and generally regards satisfaction and penal categories as juridically overloaded.

Protestant.summary: Penal substitution: Christ bears the judicial penalty due to sinners in their place.
Protestant.detail: Defenders reply that the Trinity means God is not punishing a third party but bearing the cost in himself.

Anglican.summary: Article XXXI: the offering of Christ once made is the perfect redemption and satisfaction for all sin.
Anglican.detail: The Article was aimed directly at the doctrine of the sacrifice of the Mass as then understood.

Pentecostal.summary: The atonement is proclaimed as securing forgiveness, healing, deliverance and Spirit-baptism.
Pentecostal.detail: The 'fourfold' or 'fivefold gospel' — Jesus as Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer, Spirit-Baptiser and Coming King — organises Pentecostal atonement theology.

tough_questions.question: Is faith alone enough for salvation?
tough_questions.short_answer: All traditions agree salvation is by grace and that saving faith is never barren. They differ on whether works are the fruit of justification or part of its ground.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For by grace have ye been saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, that no man should glory.

Catholic.summary: Justification is by grace through faith formed by charity; works done in grace truly merit increase of grace.
Catholic.detail: Trent's Sixth Session (1547) affirmed that we are justified freely, and simultaneously anathematised the claim that faith alone suffices.

Orthodox.summary: Salvation is a healing process of theosis; the faith/works dichotomy is regarded as a Western framing.
Orthodox.detail: Asking whether faith alone justifies is like asking whether diagnosis alone cures.

Protestant.summary: Sola fide: faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone.
Protestant.detail: James 2 is read as testing the authenticity of professed faith rather than adding a second ground.

Anglican.summary: Article XI: we are justified by faith only; Article XII: good works follow after justification.
Anglican.detail: Cranmer's Homily of Salvation is the appointed exposition.

Pentecostal.summary: Faith is evidenced by transformed life and Spirit-empowered witness; assurance is experiential as well as forensic.
Pentecostal.detail: The Wesleyan-holiness roots of the movement add a doctrine of subsequent sanctification.

tough_questions.question: Can a saved person lose salvation?
tough_questions.short_answer: Scripture holds together strong promises of preservation and severe warnings against falling away; every tradition must account for both sets of texts.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand.

Catholic.summary: Grace can be lost through mortal sin and restored through the sacrament of penance.
Catholic.detail: Assurance is real but moral rather than absolute — a confidence grounded in the sacraments rather than in introspection.

Orthodox.summary: Salvation is a lifelong path that can be abandoned; repentance is always open until death.
Orthodox.detail: The tradition's confidence is placed in continual repentance and the Church's sacramental life rather than in a decisive past moment.

Protestant.summary: Reformed teach perseverance of the saints; Arminians teach that persistent unbelief can forfeit grace.
Protestant.detail: The Canons of Dort's fifth head grants that the elect may fall grievously and for a time lose the sense of God's favour.

Anglican.summary: Article XVI: those who fall into sin after baptism may by grace rise again and amend their lives.
Anglican.detail: Article XVI was framed against both presumption and despair.

Pentecostal.summary: Most Pentecostals hold salvation can be forfeited by settled apostasy, urging continual walk in the Spirit.
Pentecostal.detail: The pastoral emphasis is on restoration of the backslidden.

tough_questions.question: What happens to those who never heard the gospel?
tough_questions.short_answer: Scripture insists God is just and that Christ is the only Saviour, while leaving the fate of the unevangelised largely to God's judgment rather than to our formula.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For when Gentiles which have no law do by nature the things of the law... they shew the work of the law written in their hearts.

Catholic.summary: Those who seek God with a sincere heart may be saved through Christ in ways known to God (Lumen Gentium 16).
Catholic.detail: Karl Rahner's 'anonymous Christian' pressed this further and remains contested.

Orthodox.summary: The Church knows where grace is, not where it is absent; judgment belongs to the merciful Christ.
Orthodox.detail: The classic formulation — 'we know where the Church is; we cannot say where she is not' — reflects a refusal to make pronouncements about the eternal destiny of individuals.

Protestant.summary: Most hold general revelation condemns but does not save, making mission urgent; a minority allow wider hope.
Protestant.detail: Romans 1 is read as establishing that general revelation renders humanity inexcusable rather than saved.

Anglican.summary: Broad range of views; the emphasis is on preaching the gospel and trusting God's justice.
Anglican.detail: What unites Anglican practice is the conviction that the question is better answered by mission than by speculation.

Pentecostal.summary: Missionary urgency dominates: the answer to the question is to go and tell.
Pentecostal.detail: The question functions in Pentecostalism chiefly as a motivator.

tough_questions.question: Is hell eternal conscious torment?
tough_questions.short_answer: All traditions affirm a real and final judgment. The debate is over the nature and duration of the punishment, not over whether judgment is real.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And these shall go away into eternal punishment: but the righteous into eternal life.

Catholic.summary: Hell is the definitive self-exclusion from communion with God, freely chosen and eternal (CCC 1033-1035).
Catholic.detail: The chief punishment is defined as eternal separation from God, in whom alone the human person can possess the life for which he was created.

Orthodox.summary: The same divine fire is joy to the saved and torment to those who reject love; the difference is in the receiver.
Orthodox.detail: Hell is therefore not a separate place of divine absence but the presence of God experienced by a soul that has refused him.

Protestant.summary: Traditionalists affirm eternal conscious punishment; annihilationists argue for final destruction from the same texts.
Protestant.detail: Annihilationists argue that 'destruction' language is more naturally read as cessation, and that immortality is a gift given to the redeemed.

Anglican.summary: Historic formularies affirm everlasting punishment; modern Anglicans hold a spectrum of views.
Anglican.detail: The 1995 Doctrine Commission report The Mystery of Salvation leaned notably away from the traditional picture.

Pentecostal.summary: Preached vividly and literally as an urgent motive for repentance and evangelism.
Pentecostal.detail: The doctrine appears in Pentecostal preaching almost always as the alternative being offered against.

tough_questions.question: Does purgatory exist?
tough_questions.short_answer: The question is whether the saved undergo a purifying process after death. All agree that nothing unclean enters God's presence; they differ on how that cleansing occurs.
tough_questions.scripture_text: If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as through fire.

Catholic.summary: Defined doctrine: a state of final purification for those who die in grace but imperfectly purified.
Catholic.detail: Purgatory is defined at Lyons (1274), Florence (1439) and Trent (1563).

Orthodox.summary: Rejects the Latin juridical model but prays for the departed and speaks of a cleansing after death.
Orthodox.detail: Yet Orthodoxy prays fervently for the departed, holds memorial services, and speaks of the soul's progress after death.

Protestant.summary: Rejected as unscriptural; Christ's blood cleanses fully and 1 Cor 3 speaks of works tested, not souls purged.
Protestant.detail: On 1 Corinthians 3, Protestants note that the fire tests works and the man is saved regardless — the passage concerns reward, not purification.

Anglican.summary: Article XXII rejects 'the Romish doctrine concerning Purgatory' as repugnant to Scripture.
Anglican.detail: Article XXII names 'Invocation of Saints' among the doctrines 'grounded upon no warranty of Scripture.'

Pentecostal.summary: Rejected outright; the believer is 'absent from the body, present with the Lord.'
Pentecostal.detail: Rejected without qualification, on the strength of 2 Corinthians 5:8 and Luke 23:43.

tough_questions.question: Should we pray to Mary and the saints?
tough_questions.short_answer: Everyone agrees Christ is the sole Mediator of redemption. The dispute is whether asking a departed saint to pray for us is intercession within the Body or a rival mediation.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For there is one God, one mediator also between God and men, himself man, Christ Jesus.

Catholic.summary: Saints are asked to intercede, not worshipped; latria belongs to God alone, dulia to the saints.
Catholic.detail: Asking a saint to pray is understood as no different in kind from asking a living Christian to pray.

Orthodox.summary: Rich invocation of the Theotokos and saints as living members of the one Body across death.
Orthodox.detail: The departed are not absent but present in the assembly, which is why icons surround the worshipper on every side.

Protestant.summary: Rejected: prayer is addressed to God alone, and no biblical warrant is found for invoking the departed.
Protestant.detail: Calvin's argument is that Scripture nowhere teaches the departed hear us.

Anglican.summary: Article XXII rejects invocation of saints; Anglo-Catholics in practice retain it, giving a divided witness.
Anglican.detail: Yet the Prayer Book calendar retains saints' days.

Pentecostal.summary: Rejected; direct access to the Father through Christ by the Spirit is emphasised.
Pentecostal.detail: The idea of an intermediary other than Christ finds no place in either its theology or its worship.

tough_questions.question: Was Mary sinless and ever-virgin?
tough_questions.short_answer: All Christians honour Mary as Theotokos, mother of the Lord. Traditions divide on the Immaculate Conception and on whether she bore other children.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And he came in unto her, and said, Hail, thou that art highly favoured, the Lord is with thee.

Catholic.summary: Immaculate Conception (1854) and perpetual virginity are defined dogmas, as is the Assumption (1950).
Catholic.detail: Pius IX defined the Immaculate Conception in Ineffabilis Deus (1854) as Mary being preserved from original sin from the first instant of conception.

Orthodox.summary: Ever-virgin and all-holy, but the Immaculate Conception as defined in the West is not received.
Orthodox.detail: Orthodoxy calls Mary Panagia (all-holy) and Achrantos (immaculate) but rejects the 1854 definition.

Protestant.summary: Mary is honoured and blessed, but held to be a sinner saved by grace; Matt 13:55 is read of true siblings.
Protestant.detail: It is worth noting that Luther, Zwingli and Calvin all personally held to her perpetual virginity.

Anglican.summary: Perpetual virginity is widely retained in the tradition; the later Marian dogmas are not required.
Anglican.detail: This is characteristic: honour retained, dogma declined.

Pentecostal.summary: Mary is respected as a model of obedient faith, without any dogmatic Marian claims.
Pentecostal.detail: Mary appears in Pentecostal teaching almost exclusively as a model of obedient faith.

tough_questions.question: Is baptism necessary for salvation?
tough_questions.short_answer: Baptism is universally commanded and never treated as optional. The division is whether it conveys regeneration or signifies a regeneration already received.
tough_questions.scripture_text: He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that disbelieveth shall be condemned.

Catholic.summary: Baptism is necessary for salvation as the ordinary means; God is not bound by his sacraments (baptism of desire/blood).
Catholic.detail: The sacrament is held to effect what it signifies ex opere operato — by the work worked.

Orthodox.summary: Baptism with chrismation is the entry into the Church and into life in Christ, normally by immersion.
Orthodox.detail: Baptism, chrismation and first communion are administered together in a single service, even to infants.

Protestant.summary: Baptists hold it an ordinance of obedience following faith; Lutherans and Reformed grant it far greater efficacy.
Protestant.detail: Lutherans hold baptismal regeneration; Baptists hold it to be an ordinance of obedience symbolising a regeneration already accomplished.

Anglican.summary: Article XXVII: a sign of regeneration or new birth, rightly administered to infants.
Anglican.detail: The Gorham Judgement of 1850 tested whether this required belief in unconditional baptismal regeneration and concluded it did not.

Pentecostal.summary: Believer's baptism by immersion, distinguished sharply from the later baptism in the Holy Spirit.
Pentecostal.detail: Believer's baptism by full immersion is the near-universal practice, understood as public confession rather than a means of grace.

tough_questions.question: Should infants be baptized?
tough_questions.short_answer: The dispute turns on whether the covenant sign belongs to households as circumcision did, or only to those who personally profess faith.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For to you is the promise, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call unto him.

Catholic.summary: Infants are baptized; original sin is remitted and the child is incorporated into Christ.
Catholic.detail: Cyprian's council of 253 debated only whether to wait until the eighth day, not whether to baptise infants at all.

Orthodox.summary: Infants are baptized, chrismated and communed at once, entering full sacramental life.
Orthodox.detail: This is why Orthodox children receive the Eucharist from infancy.

Protestant.summary: Paedobaptists appeal to household baptisms and covenant continuity; Baptists require personal profession.
Protestant.detail: Baptists reply that the new covenant is by definition a covenant of those who 'all know the LORD' (Jer 31:34).

Anglican.summary: Article XXVII commends infant baptism as most agreeable with the institution of Christ.
Anglican.detail: This two-stage structure — infant baptism followed by confirmation — is Anglicanism's attempt to hold covenant inclusion and personal profession together.

Pentecostal.summary: Infant dedication is practised instead, with baptism reserved for personal confession of faith.
Pentecostal.detail: Infant dedication — a service of thanksgiving and parental commitment without water — is the standard alternative.

tough_questions.question: What actually happens in Holy Communion?
tough_questions.short_answer: Every tradition treats the Supper as the central act of Christian worship and as a real encounter with Christ; they differ on the mode of his presence.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, This is my body, which is for you: this do in remembrance of me.

Catholic.summary: Transubstantiation: the substance of bread and wine becomes Christ's body and blood, accidents remaining.
Catholic.detail: Defined at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and elaborated at Trent.

Orthodox.summary: A true change effected by the Spirit at the epiclesis, deliberately left as mystery rather than defined.
Orthodox.detail: The change is attributed to the epiclesis — the invocation of the Spirit upon the gifts.

Protestant.summary: Lutheran sacramental union, Reformed true spiritual feeding by faith, and Zwinglian memorialism.
Protestant.detail: The Marburg Colloquy of 1529 failed on precisely this point, and the Protestant world has never reunited on it.

Anglican.summary: Article XXVIII: the body of Christ is given and received after a heavenly and spiritual manner.
Anglican.detail: The Black Rubric of 1552 further denied any 'corporal presence of Christ's natural flesh and blood.'

Pentecostal.summary: Chiefly a memorial and covenant meal, often accompanied by prayer for healing.
Pentecostal.detail: Most Pentecostal churches practise a memorial view with open communion.

tough_questions.question: Is the Bible alone sufficient, or do we need tradition?
tough_questions.short_answer: All sides use Scripture and all sides read it within a community. The question is whether tradition is a second source or the Church's servant reading of the one source.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Every scripture inspired of God is also profitable for teaching... that the man of God may be complete, furnished completely unto every good work.

Catholic.summary: Scripture and Tradition form one deposit of faith, interpreted authoritatively by the Magisterium.
Catholic.detail: Dei Verbum 9-10 teaches that Scripture and Tradition 'flow from the same divine wellspring.'

Orthodox.summary: Scripture is the supreme expression within Holy Tradition — the life of the Spirit in the Church.
Orthodox.detail: Tradition on this account is not an addition to Scripture but the Spirit's continuing life in the community that produced it.

Protestant.summary: Sola scriptura: Scripture alone is the final norm, though creeds and councils are valued as subordinate.
Protestant.detail: Calvin quotes the Fathers constantly; the point is who arbitrates when they conflict.

Anglican.summary: Scripture contains all things necessary to salvation (Article VI), read with reason and tradition.
Anglican.detail: Article VI's formula is narrower than it is often taken to be: it does not claim Scripture contains all truth.

Pentecostal.summary: Scripture is supreme, alongside a strong confidence in the Spirit's ongoing illumination and guidance.
Pentecostal.detail: Its critics identify this as the source of the movement's doctrinal volatility.

tough_questions.question: Which books belong in the Bible, and who decided?
tough_questions.short_answer: The canon was recognised rather than invented, over centuries, on grounds of apostolicity, orthodoxy and universal use. Its Old Testament boundary is still disputed.
tough_questions.scripture_text: These are my words which I spake unto you... that all things must needs be fulfilled, which are written in the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms.

Catholic.summary: Trent fixed 73 books, including the deuterocanon, as canonical and binding.
Catholic.detail: Rome's case rests on the Septuagint's wider contents, the usage of the Fathers, and the councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397).

Orthodox.summary: A slightly wider canon than Rome, with some variation between local Orthodox churches.
Orthodox.detail: The East has generally been less concerned to fix a precise list.

Protestant.summary: 66 books; the Apocrypha is read for edification but not used to establish doctrine.
Protestant.detail: The Protestant Old Testament follows the Hebrew canon Jerome preferred.

Anglican.summary: Article VI lists the canonical books and places the Apocrypha in a separate, secondary class.
Anglican.detail: This is Jerome's position adopted as formulary.

Pentecostal.summary: Follows the Protestant 66-book canon without further discussion.
Pentecostal.detail: The 66-book canon is assumed rather than argued.

tough_questions.question: Are the gifts of tongues, prophecy and healing for today?
tough_questions.short_answer: The question is whether the miraculous gifts ceased with the apostolic age or continue. All agree the Spirit remains active; they differ on the form of that activity.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Love never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall be done away... when that which is perfect is come, that which is in part shall be done away.

Catholic.summary: Charisms continue; the Catholic Charismatic Renewal is officially recognised, with discernment required.
Catholic.detail: Vatican II explicitly refused to confine charisms to the past.

Orthodox.summary: Continuing but rare and hidden, chiefly among ascetics; ecstatic public display is treated with caution.
Orthodox.detail: Prelest — spiritual delusion arising from mistaking self-generated experience for grace — is a standing category of warning.

Protestant.summary: Cessationists hold the sign gifts ceased; continuationists across the Reformed and evangelical world affirm them.
Protestant.detail: Warfield's Counterfeit Miracles (1918) gave cessationism its classic statement.

Anglican.summary: Both cessationist and charismatic streams coexist within the Communion.
Anglican.detail: The charismatic renewal reached Anglicanism through Dennis Bennett in 1960.

Pentecostal.summary: Central conviction: all gifts continue, with tongues as the initial evidence of Spirit baptism in classical teaching.
Pentecostal.detail: The restoration of the gifts is the movement's founding conviction, framed as the 'latter rain' of Joel 2:23.

tough_questions.question: Is speaking in tongues the evidence of the Holy Spirit?
tough_questions.short_answer: All agree the Spirit indwells every believer. The dispute is whether tongues is the necessary sign of a distinct post-conversion baptism in the Spirit.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.

Catholic.summary: The Spirit is given in baptism and confirmation; tongues is one charism among many, not required.
Catholic.detail: This reframing is what allowed the Renewal to be received without revising sacramental theology.

Orthodox.summary: Chrismation is the seal of the Spirit; tongues is not treated as a normative sign.
Orthodox.detail: Where extraordinary gifts appear, they are treated as personal graces rather than as evidence of an initiation not yet complete.

Protestant.summary: 1 Cor 12:30 — 'do all speak with tongues?' — is read as expecting the answer no.
Protestant.detail: Non-Pentecostal evangelicals also note that the Acts narratives describe successive stages in the gospel's spread.

Anglican.summary: Charismatic Anglicans welcome the gift while resisting the doctrine of initial evidence.
Anglican.detail: Preferring to speak of being filled with the Spirit — a repeatable command in Ephesians 5:18.

Pentecostal.summary: Classical Pentecostalism teaches tongues as the initial physical evidence of Spirit baptism.
Pentecostal.detail: Formulated at Charles Parham's Bethel Bible School in Topeka on 1 January 1901.

tough_questions.question: Can women be pastors, priests or preachers?
tough_questions.short_answer: All agree women share fully in salvation and in gifting for ministry. The dispute concerns the office of ordained governing and teaching authority.
tough_questions.scripture_text: There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus.

Catholic.summary: Ordination to the priesthood is reserved to men, taught as definitively held (Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994).
Catholic.detail: Women nonetheless hold significant offices, including as Doctors of the Church.

Orthodox.summary: An exclusively male priesthood; the ancient order of deaconess is discussed for possible restoration.
Orthodox.detail: The order of deaconess, however, is historically attested with its own ordination rite.

Protestant.summary: Egalitarians ordain women freely; complementarians restrict the eldership while affirming wide ministry.
Protestant.detail: Both camps contain serious exegetes, and the divide runs through most evangelical denominations.

Anglican.summary: Most provinces ordain women, including as bishops; some provinces and parishes do not.
Anglican.detail: Women were first ordained priest in Hong Kong in 1944 and 1971, in the United States in 1974, in England in 1994.

Pentecostal.summary: Historically among the earliest to license and ordain women preachers, with practice varying by denomination.
Pentecostal.detail: Aimee Semple McPherson founded a denomination in 1927.

tough_questions.question: Is divorce and remarriage ever permitted?
tough_questions.short_answer: All hold marriage to be a lifelong covenant and divorce a grievous evil. They differ on whether any exception permits remarriage while the spouse lives.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And I say unto you, Whosoever shall put away his wife, except for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery.

Catholic.summary: A consummated sacramental marriage is indissoluble; annulment declares no valid marriage ever existed.
Catholic.detail: Amoris Laetitia (2016) opened a contested pastoral path to communion for some of the divorced and remarried.

Orthodox.summary: Permits remarriage by oikonomia, with a penitential rather than festal second rite.
Orthodox.detail: The East permits up to three marriages, applying oikonomia — pastoral accommodation to human weakness.

Protestant.summary: Most allow remarriage after adultery or desertion (Matt 19:9; 1 Cor 7:15); some allow none.
Protestant.detail: Stricter Reformed and Anabaptist traditions permit separation but no remarriage while both parties live.

Anglican.summary: Practice varies widely by province; remarriage in church is often permitted with pastoral review.
Anglican.detail: The abdication crisis of 1936 remains the most public instance of the older discipline.

Pentecostal.summary: Generally permits remarriage on the biblical grounds, with restrictions often applied to ministers.
Pentecostal.detail: Most Pentecostal bodies permit remarriage on the biblical grounds while applying stricter standards to ministers.

tough_questions.question: What does the Bible say about homosexuality?
tough_questions.short_answer: The historic Christian teaching restricts sexual union to marriage between a man and a woman, while insisting on the equal dignity of every person and rejecting contempt or cruelty.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And such were some of you: but ye were washed, but ye were sanctified, but ye were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Spirit of our God.

Catholic.summary: Homosexual acts are gravely disordered, while persons must be accepted with respect, compassion and sensitivity (CCC 2357-2359).
Catholic.detail: The Catechism distinguishes inclination from act, calls the inclination objectively disordered but not itself sinful.

Orthodox.summary: Holds the traditional teaching without variation, framed pastorally within confession and repentance.
Orthodox.detail: The framework is therapeutic — all disordered desire, of whatever kind, is material for repentance and healing.

Protestant.summary: Traditionalists maintain the historic position; affirming denominations have revised it, causing major division.
Protestant.detail: Affirming scholars argue the biblical texts address exploitative or idolatrous practices unknown to covenanted partnership.

Anglican.summary: The most publicly contested issue in the Communion, with provinces sharply divided.
Anglican.detail: The Communion is genuinely divided since Lambeth 1998's Resolution I.10.

Pentecostal.summary: Overwhelmingly traditional, coupled with strong emphasis on deliverance, transformation and welcome to repentance.
Pentecostal.detail: The movement's global centre of gravity in Africa, Latin America and Asia makes any revision extremely unlikely.

tough_questions.question: Is the Sabbath Saturday or Sunday?
tough_questions.short_answer: Christians gathered on the first day from the earliest records, marking the resurrection. Whether that transfers the fourth commandment or fulfils it is the point at issue.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of a feast day or a new moon or a sabbath day: which are a shadow of the things to come; but the body is Christ's.

Catholic.summary: The Lord's Day fulfils the Sabbath; Sunday obligation is Church law rooted in the resurrection.
Catholic.detail: Sunday obligation is canon law (CIC 1247) rather than divine law transferred from the Decalogue.

Orthodox.summary: Saturday retains liturgical honour, but Sunday is the day of resurrection and eucharistic assembly.
Orthodox.detail: Saturday is the only day of Great Lent on which the full Liturgy is celebrated.

Protestant.summary: Sabbatarians treat Sunday as the Christian Sabbath; others see the Sabbath fulfilled in Christ's rest.
Protestant.detail: Lutherans and most continental Reformed reject the transfer, following Calvin's view that the Sabbath was ceremonial.

Anglican.summary: The Lord's Day is kept with the moral principle of the fourth commandment retained.
Anglican.detail: Anglican practice historically kept Sunday strictly without adopting full Puritan sabbatarianism.

Pentecostal.summary: Sunday worship without Sabbatarian legalism; the emphasis is on gathering, not the calendar.
Pentecostal.detail: Seventh-day Adventism's Saturday claim prompted extensive Pentecostal responses in the early twentieth century.

tough_questions.question: Should Christians tithe ten percent?
tough_questions.short_answer: Generous, sacrificial and regular giving is commanded everywhere in the New Testament; whether the specific ten percent figure carries over from the Law is disputed.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Let each man do according as he hath purposed in his heart: not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.

Catholic.summary: No fixed tithe is imposed; the faithful must support the Church according to their means.
Catholic.detail: The medieval tithe was a civil as much as ecclesiastical levy, abolished in most countries in the nineteenth century.

Orthodox.summary: Giving is encouraged as stewardship and almsgiving rather than as a legislated percentage.
Orthodox.detail: The fathers speak of surplus wealth as belonging by right to the poor.

Protestant.summary: Many teach the tithe as a baseline; others hold it fulfilled and replaced by grace-motivated proportional giving.
Protestant.detail: Reformed critics note that Malachi 3:10 addresses a covenant nation under a theocratic law.

Anglican.summary: Proportional giving is commended, with the tithe often taught as a guideline, not a rule.
Anglican.detail: The Church of England's stewardship programmes historically suggested five percent to the church and five percent to charity.

Pentecostal.summary: The tithe is strongly and often literally taught, frequently with Malachi 3:10 as its charter.
Pentecostal.detail: Prosperity-influenced teaching on this point has drawn sustained criticism from within the movement itself.

tough_questions.question: Is it wrong to use images or icons in worship?
tough_questions.short_answer: All reject the worship of any created thing. The dispute is whether veneration passing through an image to its prototype is idolatry or legitimate honour.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Thou shalt not make unto thee a graven image, nor any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath.

Catholic.summary: Images are permitted and honoured; the honour passes to the person represented (Second Nicaea, 787).
Catholic.detail: Second Nicaea distinguished proskynesis (veneration) from latreia (worship), and grounded images in the Incarnation.

Orthodox.summary: Icons are dogmatically defended as a consequence of the Incarnation; iconoclasm was condemned as heresy.
Orthodox.detail: Iconoclasm was defeated twice, and the Triumph of Orthodoxy on the first Sunday of Lent still commemorates the restoration of icons in 843.

Protestant.summary: Reformed traditions removed images as violating the second commandment; Lutherans retained many.
Protestant.detail: Calvin devoted Institutes I.11 to the argument that the human mind is a perpetual factory of idols.

Anglican.summary: A middle path: images are permitted as ornament and teaching, but not to be worshipped.
Anglican.detail: Anglo-Catholic parishes today are richly furnished.

Pentecostal.summary: Generally avoids religious imagery altogether, preferring bare worship space.
Pentecostal.detail: The practice reflects inherited free-church custom rather than an articulated iconoclastic theology.

tough_questions.question: Do Christians still have to keep the Old Testament law?
tough_questions.short_answer: The moral character of God's law abides while the ceremonial and civil order given to Israel finds its fulfilment in Christ.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness to every one that believeth.

Catholic.summary: The Decalogue binds; ceremonial precepts are abrogated and fulfilled in the sacraments.
Catholic.detail: Aquinas' threefold division of moral, ceremonial and judicial precepts (Summa I-II, Q.99) remains the standard Catholic framework.

Orthodox.summary: The law is read typologically and liturgically as preparation, not as a continuing code.
Orthodox.detail: The East reads the Law typologically through the liturgy.

Protestant.summary: The threefold division — moral, ceremonial, civil — is standard; dispensationalists press discontinuity further.
Protestant.detail: The Reformed confessions adopt the threefold division explicitly (Westminster XIX).

Anglican.summary: Article VII: no Christian is bound to the ceremonies and rites, but no man is free from the commandments called Moral.
Anglican.detail: Article VII states the position exactly.

Pentecostal.summary: Grace-centred, with strong practical moral teaching drawn from both Testaments.
Pentecostal.detail: Holiness teaching inherited from the Wesleyan tradition maintains rigorous practical standards.

tough_questions.question: What is the unforgivable sin?
tough_questions.short_answer: In context it is the deliberate attribution of the Spirit's evident work to Satan — a settled and knowing rejection, not a fearful doubt.
tough_questions.scripture_text: But whosoever shall blasphem e against the Holy Spirit hath never forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin.

Catholic.summary: Final impenitence — the refusal of mercy itself, which cannot be forgiven because it declines forgiveness.
Catholic.detail: The sin is unforgivable not because God's mercy is exhausted but because it is refused (CCC 1864).

Orthodox.summary: A hardened state of the heart; while there is life there is repentance, so despair is itself the danger.
Orthodox.detail: Isaac the Syrian's dictum that there is no sin that overcomes God's mercy is standard.

Protestant.summary: A definitive, knowing rejection of the Spirit's testimony to Christ, not any single lapse.
Protestant.detail: The sin cannot be committed by anyone who fears having committed it.

Anglican.summary: Handled pastorally: the troubled conscience is reassured rather than examined for the sin.
Anglican.detail: Anglican moral theology has a developed literature on scrupulosity.

Pentecostal.summary: Taught with warning against mocking the Spirit's manifest work, alongside strong assurance to the fearful.
Pentecostal.detail: Pastors likewise reassure the troubled that the fear itself is evidence against guilt.

tough_questions.question: Can Christians be demon-possessed?
tough_questions.short_answer: All affirm the reality of the demonic and the greater power of Christ. The debate is whether a believer indwelt by the Spirit can be possessed, as against oppressed or harassed.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Ye are of God, my little children, and have overcome them: because greater is he that is in you than he that is in the world.

Catholic.summary: Exorcism is a reserved rite; the baptized may be gravely oppressed but possession of the soul is contested.
Catholic.detail: The Church requires medical and psychiatric evaluation first.

Orthodox.summary: Prayers of exorcism are part of the baptismal rite itself; deliverance is ordinary pastoral care.
Orthodox.detail: Ongoing struggle is addressed through confession, fasting and the Jesus Prayer.

Protestant.summary: Most distinguish oppression from possession, holding that the Spirit's indwelling excludes the latter.
Protestant.detail: Reformed writers tend to emphasise the sufficiency of ordinary means — Word, prayer, sacrament, community.

Anglican.summary: A ministry of deliverance exists under episcopal authorisation, carefully regulated.
Anglican.detail: Each Church of England diocese appoints an adviser for deliverance ministry.

Pentecostal.summary: Deliverance ministry is widespread; many teach that believers can be demonised in body or soul though not owned.
Pentecostal.detail: Many teach that a Christian can be 'demonised' in areas of unrepented sin or unhealed trauma.

tough_questions.question: Does God still speak outside the Bible?
tough_questions.short_answer: Christ is God's final and sufficient word. Whether God gives further non-canonical guidance — and how it is tested — divides the traditions.
tough_questions.scripture_text: God, having of old time spoken unto the fathers in the prophets by divers portions and in divers manners, hath at the end of these days spoken unto us in his Son.

Catholic.summary: Public revelation closed with the apostles; private revelation may be approved but binds no one.
Catholic.detail: Approved private revelations are declared 'worthy of belief' but cannot add to or correct the deposit of faith (CCC 66-67).

Orthodox.summary: The Spirit speaks through the Church's life, the saints and the councils, never against Scripture.
Orthodox.detail: Nothing is received that stands in tension with Scripture and the councils.

Protestant.summary: Cessationists limit guidance to Scripture and providence; continuationists allow subordinate prophetic words.
Protestant.detail: Wayne Grudem argues that New Testament congregational prophecy is a fallible, testable gift categorically different from Scripture.

Anglican.summary: Scripture is the norm; discernment is exercised communally and cautiously.
Anglican.detail: Anglicanism moves slowly on contested questions by design.

Pentecostal.summary: Expects prophecy, dreams and words of knowledge, all subject to the written Word.
Pentecostal.detail: Prophecy, dreams, visions and words of knowledge are expected in ordinary church life.

tough_questions.question: Is predestination fair?
tough_questions.short_answer: Election is taught plainly in Scripture and so is God's genuine desire that none perish. Every system must hold both, and each does so differently.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why didst thou make me thus?

Catholic.summary: God predestines to glory without predestining anyone to sin; grace and freedom cooperate.
Catholic.detail: The Church has refused to adjudicate between Thomist and Molinist accounts of how this works.

Orthodox.summary: Election is corporate and foreknowing; God's will to save all is unqualified.
Orthodox.detail: Predestination is understood as God's foreknowing love, not as a prior selection.

Protestant.summary: Calvinists affirm unconditional election; Arminians hold election conditional on foreseen faith.
Protestant.detail: Dort's five heads answered the Remonstrants point by point.

Anglican.summary: Article XVII calls predestination 'full of sweet, pleasant, and unspeakable comfort' to the godly.
Anglican.detail: Article XVII is a masterpiece of deliberate reticence.

Pentecostal.summary: Predominantly Arminian, emphasising a whosoever-will gospel.
Pentecostal.detail: The movement is overwhelmingly Arminian, and altar-call preaching presupposes genuine contingency.

tough_questions.question: How do we reconcile Genesis with modern science?
tough_questions.short_answer: Genesis answers who and why rather than the mechanism and rate. Christians divide over the genre and chronology of the days while agreeing God is the sole Creator.
tough_questions.scripture_text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

Catholic.summary: Evolution is compatible with faith provided the soul is directly created by God (Humani Generis).
Catholic.detail: John Paul II in 1996 called evolution 'more than a hypothesis.'

Orthodox.summary: Genesis is read patristically and liturgically; literalism is not required and rarely pressed.
Orthodox.detail: Basil's Hexaemeron is fairly literal, Origen and Gregory of Nyssa markedly allegorical.

Protestant.summary: Young-earth, old-earth and framework readings coexist and contend within evangelicalism.
Protestant.detail: Young-earth creationism as a movement dates largely from Whitcomb and Morris' The Genesis Flood (1961).

Anglican.summary: Broadly accepts mainstream science while confessing God as Creator.
Anglican.detail: Frederick Temple, later Archbishop of Canterbury, defended evolution in 1884.

Pentecostal.summary: Often literal in popular teaching, though views vary widely across the movement.
Pentecostal.detail: The movement has no confessional position on the question.

tough_questions.question: Was Adam a real historical person?
tough_questions.short_answer: Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 parallels Adam with Christ, which is why the historicity question carries doctrinal weight rather than merely historical interest.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Therefore, as through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin; and so death passed unto all men, for that all sinned.

Catholic.summary: Polygenism is problematic for original sin; a real first couple or at least a real first sin is required.
Catholic.detail: Humani Generis raised difficulties for polygenism precisely because original sin is transmitted by descent.

Orthodox.summary: Adam is a real person and also the archetype of all humanity; the fall is genuinely historical.
Orthodox.detail: Because the East frames the fall in terms of inherited mortality and corruption rather than inherited guilt.

Protestant.summary: Conservatives insist on historicity; some evangelical scholars propose archetypal readings, contested sharply.
Protestant.detail: Proposals such as John Walton's archetypal reading and Denis Alexander's have been vigorously contested.

Anglican.summary: Ranges from literal to symbolic; the doctrine of universal sinfulness is retained either way.
Anglican.detail: No formulary requires a literal Adam.

Pentecostal.summary: Historic Adam is assumed as a matter of course.
Pentecostal.detail: The question has attracted little formal Pentecostal reflection.

tough_questions.question: Is suicide an unforgivable sin?
tough_questions.short_answer: The historic instinct that suicide forecloses repentance has been tempered by understanding of mental illness and by the recognition that no sin outruns the cross.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life... shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Catholic.summary: Grave matter, but grave psychological factors can diminish culpability; the Church prays and does not despair (CCC 2282-2283).
Catholic.detail: The Church prays for such persons, holding that God can provide opportunity for repentance in ways known to him alone.

Orthodox.summary: Historically restricted funeral rites, now widely relaxed where illness is evident, with prayer for mercy.
Orthodox.detail: Memorial prayers are offered.

Protestant.summary: Held to be sin but not unforgivable; salvation rests on Christ's work, not on the last conscious act.
Protestant.detail: The pastoral emphasis has shifted decisively toward mental-health literacy.

Anglican.summary: Full Christian burial is given, with strong pastoral care for the bereaved.
Anglican.detail: The 1662 rubric denying burial rites was effectively abandoned.

Pentecostal.summary: Generally taught as sin with hope, alongside emphasis on deliverance, counsel and community.
Pentecostal.detail: Growing emphasis on counselling, community and destigmatisation.

tough_questions.question: Is abortion always wrong?
tough_questions.short_answer: The Christian tradition has consistently opposed abortion from the earliest centuries, while differing on hard cases where the mother's life is directly threatened.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For thou didst form my inward parts: thou didst cover me in my mother's womb.

Catholic.summary: Direct abortion is gravely wrong from conception; the principle of double effect governs life-threatening cases.
Catholic.detail: Canon 1398 attaches automatic excommunication to procuring abortion.

Orthodox.summary: Condemned as taking innocent life, with pastoral economy applied in extreme circumstances.
Orthodox.detail: The Didache's 'thou shalt not murder a child by abortion' (c. AD 100) is regularly cited.

Protestant.summary: Nearly all conservative traditions oppose it; some mainline bodies permit wider exceptions.
Protestant.detail: Evangelical opposition consolidated in the 1970s and 80s.

Anglican.summary: Officially opposes abortion while allowing narrow exceptions; provinces vary considerably.
Anglican.detail: Provinces in the Global South are generally more restrictive.

Pentecostal.summary: Strongly pro-life, with growing emphasis on practical support for mothers.
Pentecostal.detail: The practical emphasis increasingly on crisis-pregnancy support, adoption and post-abortion pastoral care.

tough_questions.question: Can Christians serve in war or take a life?
tough_questions.short_answer: The Church has produced both a robust just-war tradition and a continuous pacifist witness; both claim the Sermon on the Mount.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called sons of God.

Catholic.summary: A developed just-war doctrine with strict conditions, alongside growing emphasis on peacebuilding.
Catholic.detail: Francis has questioned whether modern warfare can meet the criteria at all.

Orthodox.summary: War is never blessed as good; soldiers were historically given penance even for lawful killing.
Orthodox.detail: Basil's Canon 13 recommended that soldiers who had killed abstain from communion for three years.

Protestant.summary: Just war predominates; Anabaptists, Mennonites and Quakers maintain principled non-resistance.
Protestant.detail: Luther's Whether Soldiers Too Can Be Saved and the Reformed tradition affirm just war.

Anglican.summary: Article XXXVII permits Christians to bear weapons and serve in just wars at the magistrate's command.
Anglican.detail: Anglican pacifism nonetheless has a distinguished modern lineage.

Pentecostal.summary: Early Pentecostals were often pacifist; most bodies later accepted military service.
Pentecostal.detail: The position was quietly reversed during the Second World War.

tough_questions.question: How should Christians relate to government?
tough_questions.short_answer: Submission to lawful authority is commanded, and so is refusal when the state commands what God forbids — 'we must obey God rather than men.'
tough_questions.scripture_text: Let every soul be in subjection to the higher powers: for there is no power but of God; and the powers that be are ordained of God.

Catholic.summary: Catholic social teaching: subsidiarity, solidarity, the common good, and conscientious objection where required.
Catholic.detail: Catholic social teaching runs from Rerum Novarum (1891) to the present.

Orthodox.summary: Historic symphonia between church and state, complicated in practice by nationalism.
Orthodox.detail: Its historical vulnerability has been capture by the state.

Protestant.summary: Two-kingdoms and Kuyperian sphere-sovereignty models; strong tradition of lawful resistance to tyranny.
Protestant.detail: The Barmen Declaration (1934) is the classic modern statement of the limits of obedience.

Anglican.summary: Established in England, yet holding the monarch under God and the law.
Anglican.detail: Establishment gives the Church of England bishops seats in the House of Lords.

Pentecostal.summary: Historically apolitical and separatist; now widely politically engaged in many nations.
Pentecostal.detail: Political engagement has grown dramatically in Brazil, Nigeria, Guatemala and the United States.

tough_questions.question: Is wealth a blessing or a danger?
tough_questions.short_answer: Scripture treats possessions as a stewardship and a spiritual hazard at once. It never condemns wealth as such, and never leaves it unexamined.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil: which some reaching after have been led astray from the faith.

Catholic.summary: The universal destination of goods and a preferential option for the poor; private property is legitimate but not absolute.
Catholic.detail: The universal destination of goods holds that creation is given to all.

Orthodox.summary: Strong ascetic and almsgiving tradition; luxury is treated as a spiritual illness.
Orthodox.detail: Basil the Great's homilies are unsparing: the bread you hold belongs to the hungry.

Protestant.summary: The Protestant work ethic alongside sharp critique of greed; prosperity teaching is widely rejected.
Protestant.detail: The Lausanne Movement has formally repudiated prosperity teaching.

Anglican.summary: Stewardship and social responsibility, with a long tradition of institutional charity.
Anglican.detail: William Temple's Christianity and Social Order (1942) influenced the post-war welfare settlement.

Pentecostal.summary: Deeply divided: prosperity streams contend with strong holiness and simplicity traditions.
Pentecostal.detail: Prosperity teaching is enormously influential in parts of Africa and Latin America.

tough_questions.question: What is the church — building, denomination, or people?
tough_questions.short_answer: The Church is the people of God, the body of Christ, and the temple of the Spirit — never merely an institution or a venue, though it takes visible form.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Ye also, as living stones, are built up a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices.

Catholic.summary: The one Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, visibly structured under the bishops with the Pope.
Catholic.detail: Lumen Gentium presents the Church first as the People of God and only then as hierarchy.

Orthodox.summary: The Church is the eucharistic assembly gathered around its bishop, one and undivided.
Orthodox.detail: Eucharistic ecclesiology holds that the whole Church is fully present in each local assembly.

Protestant.summary: The invisible church of all true believers, made visible wherever the Word and sacraments are rightly handled.
Protestant.detail: The distinction between visible and invisible church allows the true church to be acknowledged across institutional boundaries.

Anglican.summary: Article XIX: a congregation of faithful men in which the pure Word is preached and the sacraments duly ministered.
Anglican.detail: Article XIX pointedly adds that Jerusalem, Alexandria, Antioch and Rome have all erred.

Pentecostal.summary: The Spirit-filled body of believers; institutional structure is held loosely.
Pentecostal.detail: The movement's rapid multiplication of independent congregations is a direct consequence of this ecclesiology.

tough_questions.question: Is there salvation outside the church?
tough_questions.short_answer: The ancient maxim extra ecclesiam nulla salus is affirmed in some sense by all, but the definition of 'church' does the decisive work.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And in none other is there salvation: for neither is there any other name under heaven, that is given among men, wherein we must be saved.

Catholic.summary: Those outside may be joined to the Church in ways known to God; other communities have real but imperfect communion.
Catholic.detail: Cyprian's extra ecclesiam nulla salus is retained but interpreted through Lumen Gentium 14-16.

Orthodox.summary: The Church's boundaries are known where grace is; beyond them the Church declines to pronounce.
Orthodox.detail: Orthodox writers frequently quote the principle that the Church's limits are known to God alone.

Protestant.summary: Salvation is by union with Christ, which constitutes membership in the true invisible church.
Protestant.detail: This is the ecclesiological ground of evangelical trans-denominational cooperation.

Anglican.summary: Recognises the ecclesial reality of other Christian bodies while maintaining its own order.
Anglican.detail: The Chicago-Lambeth Quadrilateral (1888) names Scripture, the Creeds, the two dominical sacraments and the historic episcopate.

Pentecostal.summary: Personal relationship with Christ is decisive; denominational membership is secondary.
Pentecostal.detail: Pentecostals have generally cooperated freely across denominational lines.

tough_questions.question: What is the purpose of suffering for a believer?
tough_questions.short_answer: Suffering is never called good in itself, but God is repeatedly shown using it to form character, deepen dependence and conform believers to Christ.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And he hath said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness.

Catholic.summary: Redemptive suffering: believers may unite their sufferings with Christ's for the good of the Body (Col 1:24).
Catholic.detail: John Paul II's Salvifici Doloris (1984) is the fullest modern treatment.

Orthodox.summary: Suffering is purifying and theotic, borne with the saints and the martyrs.
Orthodox.detail: The tradition speaks of bearing one's cross as participation in Christ.

Protestant.summary: Sanctifying discipline from a loving Father, never penal for the justified.
Protestant.detail: Luther's theology of the cross adds that God works through apparent contradiction.

Anglican.summary: Framed liturgically through Lent, the Passion and a theology of the cross.
Anglican.detail: Anglican spiritual writers from Donne to Austin Farrer have treated affliction as a principal theme.

Pentecostal.summary: Suffering is real but often resisted in prayer; healing is sought while endurance is honoured.
Pentecostal.detail: Pentecostal scholars have addressed this directly in recent decades.

tough_questions.question: Does God heal today, and why are some not healed?
tough_questions.short_answer: All traditions pray for the sick and confess that God heals. None can guarantee the timing, and Scripture itself records unhealed servants of God.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Is any among you sick? let him call for the elders of the church... and the prayer of faith shall save him that is sick.

Catholic.summary: Anointing of the sick is a sacrament for healing of body and soul, and preparation for death.
Catholic.detail: Since Vatican II it is no longer restricted to the dying.

Orthodox.summary: Holy Unction is administered widely, especially in Holy Week, for all the faithful.
Orthodox.detail: Healing is treated as a normal part of the Church's life rather than an emergency measure.

Protestant.summary: Prayer for healing is affirmed; most reject any guarantee, holding God's will to be sovereign.
Protestant.detail: Reformed writers stress that God's sovereign will governs the outcome.

Anglican.summary: Healing services and anointing are practised within a sacramental and pastoral framework.
Anglican.detail: Services of healing with laying on of hands and anointing are provided in Common Worship.

Pentecostal.summary: Divine healing is a core doctrine, often tied to the atonement, with unanswered prayer a live pastoral question.
Pentecostal.detail: Divine healing is one of the movement's founding doctrines.

tough_questions.question: What is the baptism in the Holy Spirit?
tough_questions.short_answer: Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion. Whether there is a distinct subsequent empowering, and what marks it, is the dividing question.
tough_questions.scripture_text: For John indeed baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence.

Catholic.summary: The Spirit is given in baptism and confirmation; the charismatic renewal speaks of a release of that grace.
Catholic.detail: The Renewal's language of 'baptism in the Spirit' is officially interpreted as a release of sacramental grace already given.

Orthodox.summary: Chrismation confers the seal of the gift of the Spirit at initiation.
Orthodox.detail: The East sees the Western separation of confirmation from baptism as an unfortunate historical accident.

Protestant.summary: Usually identified with conversion itself; subsequent fillings are affirmed without a second baptism.
Protestant.detail: Lloyd-Jones represents a significant exception, teaching a distinct experience of assurance.

Anglican.summary: Confirmation is linked to the Spirit's strengthening; charismatic Anglicans add experiential emphasis.
Anglican.detail: Charismatic Anglicans typically speak of being filled rather than baptised.

Pentecostal.summary: A distinct subsequent experience for power in witness, classically evidenced by speaking in tongues.
Pentecostal.detail: The doctrine explains the movement's characteristic two-stage spirituality: conversion, then empowerment for witness.

tough_questions.question: Is the rapture biblical, and when does it occur?
tough_questions.short_answer: All Christians confess Christ will return bodily and gather his people. Whether that gathering is a separate event before a tribulation is a modern and contested question.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Then we that are alive, that are left, shall together with them be caught up in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air.

Catholic.summary: No separate rapture; the 'catching up' is part of the one general resurrection at the Second Coming.
Catholic.detail: There is no distinct rapture in Catholic eschatology.

Orthodox.summary: The same: one return, one judgment; dispensational schemes are absent from the tradition.
Orthodox.detail: The East regards detailed prophetic charting with considerable suspicion.

Protestant.summary: Dispensationalists teach a pre-tribulation rapture; Reformed and most others hold a single return.
Protestant.detail: The pre-tribulation rapture was popularised by J. N. Darby from the 1830s.

Anglican.summary: Follows the creedal single return; the popular rapture scheme is rarely taught.
Anglican.detail: The rapture as a separate event is essentially unknown in Anglican formularies.

Pentecostal.summary: Pre-tribulation rapture is widely and vividly preached in classical Pentecostal circles.
Pentecostal.detail: The movement contains post-tribulational voices and the question is rarely made a test of fellowship.

tough_questions.question: Who is the Antichrist?
tough_questions.short_answer: John uses the term for any spirit denying that Jesus is the Christ come in flesh; Paul speaks of a coming man of sin. Both a present spirit and a final figure are in view.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Little children, it is the last hour: and as ye heard that antichrist cometh, even now have there arisen many antichrists.

Catholic.summary: A final adversary is expected, though the Church declines to identify him with any living person.
Catholic.detail: The Catechism speaks of a deception of religious appearance — 'a pseudo-messianism by which man glorifies himself in place of God.'

Orthodox.summary: Expects a personal antichrist at the end; identification is discouraged as speculation.
Orthodox.detail: Orthodox eschatological literature discusses him at length, but warns strongly against date-setting and identification.

Protestant.summary: Reformers often identified the papacy; most modern evangelicals expect a future individual.
Protestant.detail: Modern evangelical futurism generally expects an individual world ruler.

Anglican.summary: Historic polemic has been largely set aside in favour of ecumenical relations.
Anglican.detail: ARCIC dialogue proceeds on entirely different terms.

Pentecostal.summary: Commonly expects a literal end-times world ruler, tied to prophetic teaching.
Pentecostal.detail: Identification attempts recur in popular Pentecostal literature and are regularly disowned by its scholars.

tough_questions.question: Will there be a literal new earth?
tough_questions.short_answer: The Christian hope is not escape from matter but the renewal of it — a resurrected body on a restored earth, not disembodied souls in a distant sky.
tough_questions.scripture_text: And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth are passed away.

Catholic.summary: The material creation will be renewed and transfigured, not annihilated (CCC 1042-1050).
Catholic.detail: CCC 1047 teaches that the visible universe is itself destined to be transformed.

Orthodox.summary: The cosmos is transfigured and deified; creation shares the glory of the resurrection.
Orthodox.detail: Maximus the Confessor's vision of all things gathered up in Christ underlies the Eastern account.

Protestant.summary: Renewal is increasingly emphasised over destruction, recovering Romans 8 and Isaiah 65.
Protestant.detail: N. T. Wright has recovered new-creation eschatology against a popular piety of disembodied heaven.

Anglican.summary: Confessed in the Creed's 'life of the world to come,' with a strong incarnational theology.
Anglican.detail: The burial office's sure and certain hope of resurrection expresses this.

Pentecostal.summary: Held literally, often with vivid expectation of a restored physical earth.
Pentecostal.detail: The emphasis is on restoration of what was lost in Eden.

tough_questions.question: Are other religions entirely false?
tough_questions.short_answer: Christianity claims Christ as uniquely and universally the Saviour, which does not require denying every true or good thing found elsewhere.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, and the truth, and the life: no one cometh unto the Father, but by me.

Catholic.summary: Other religions may contain elements of truth and moral good, but only Catholicism possesses the full means of salvation.
Catholic.detail: Dominus Iesus (2000) reasserted that salvation is through Christ and the Church.

Orthodox.summary: Other religions are regarded as lacking the fullness of truth found in Orthodox Christianity.
Orthodox.detail: Dialogue is encouraged, but claims of equal truth are not accepted.

Protestant.summary: Christ is the only way of salvation; other religions contain error but may have elements of truth.
Protestant.detail: Evangelical exclusivism holds that salvation is only through explicit faith in Christ.

Anglican.summary: Broad range of views; typically affirms Christ's uniqueness while engaging other religions respectfully.
Anglican.detail: Anglicanism generally prefers dialogue over confrontation.

Pentecostal.summary: Affirms Christ as the only way, with strong missionary mandate to all nations.
Pentecostal.detail: Pentecostal missions have been remarkably effective across cultures worldwide.

tough_questions.question: How can we trust the Bible when manuscripts differ?
tough_questions.short_answer: The differences are overwhelmingly minor spelling variations, word order, and obvious scribal slips. No Christian doctrine rests on a contested reading.
tough_questions.scripture_text: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.

Catholic.summary: The Church discerns the authentic text and preserves it; minor variants do not threaten core doctrines.
Catholic.detail: Catholic scholars actively participate in textual criticism.

Orthodox.summary: The Spirit has preserved the Church's access to Scripture's meaning across centuries.
Orthodox.detail: Orthodox churches use traditional texts while acknowledging manuscript diversity.

Protestant.summary: The science of textual criticism shows remarkable textual fidelity across thousands of manuscripts.
Protestant.detail: The Dead Sea Scrolls confirmed the reliability of the Hebrew text.

Anglican.summary: Anglicanism accepts the findings of textual criticism while maintaining biblical authority.
Anglican.detail: No article of faith depends on a disputed reading.

Pentecostal.summary: The Bible is God's inspired Word; textual variations do not undermine its message.
Pentecostal.detail: Pentecostal scholarship increasingly engages in textual and higher criticism.
